name: Severe Immune-Mediated Enteropathy

diagnosticCriteria.formalCriteriaName: Proposed Diagnostic Criteria for Severe Immune-Mediated Enteropathy

criteria.description: Persistent, severe, non-infectious diarrhea lasting more than 4 weeks
Histological evidence of severe villous atrophy with crypt hyperplasia and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes on small bowel biopsy
Presence of circulating anti-enterocyte or anti-goblet cell autoantibodies
Exclusion of infectious, neoplastic, and other known causes of enteropathy
Clinical and histological improvement following immunosuppressive therapy

diagnosticCriteria.minimumForDiagnosis: All major criteria must be met including chronic severe diarrhea, characteristic biopsy findings, presence of autoantibodies, and exclusion of other causes.
diagnosticCriteria.notes: Diagnosis requires multidisciplinary evaluation including gastroenterology, pathology, and immunology.

pathognomonic.symptomName: Severe villous atrophy on small bowel biopsy
searchTerms: severe damage to small intestine lining

common.symptomName: Nutritional deficiencies (e.g. iron, folate, vitamin B12)
searchTerms: low iron, folate, or B12 levels

common.symptomName: Failure to thrive in pediatric patients
searchTerms: failure to gain weight and grow

occasional.symptomName: Fat-soluble vitamin deficiencies (A, D, E, K)
searchTerms: lack of vitamins A, D, E, K

occasional.symptomName: Peripheral edema due to protein loss
searchTerms: fluid buildup in limbs from low protein
peripheral swelling related to protein deficiency
low red blood cells from chronic illness
chronic disease causing low blood count

rare.symptomName: Neurological manifestations secondary to vitamin deficiencies (e.g. peripheral neuropathy)

searchTerms: itchy blistering rash like dermatitis herpetiformis
rash similar to celiac disease skin symptoms

rare.symptomName: Refractory hypokalemia due to chronic diarrhea

laboratory: Elevated anti-enterocyte and anti-goblet cell autoantibodies
Micronutrient deficiencies (iron, folate, vitamin B12, fat-soluble vitamins)
imaging: Small bowel imaging may show mucosal thickening or atrophy but is nonspecific
genetic: No specific genetic mutation identified; possible association with HLA-DQ2/DQ8 haplotypes in some cases
other: Small bowel biopsy showing severe villous atrophy, crypt hyperplasia, and increased intraepithelial lymphocytes
Exclusion of infectious etiologies by stool studies and cultures

distinguishingFeatures: Less severe villous atrophy compared to severe immune-mediated enteropathy
History of travel to endemic areas
Poor response to immunosuppressive therapy alone

redFlags: Severe, persistent diarrhea unresponsive to standard therapies
Rapid weight loss and severe malnutrition
Presence of anti-enterocyte autoantibodies with villous atrophy
references: Akram S, Murray JA. Autoimmune enteropathy: clinical and immunologic features and response to therapy. Clin Gastroenterol Hepatol. 2007.
Unsworth DJ, Walker-Smith JA. Autoimmune enteropathy in children. Gut. 1985.
